questions.question:
The engineering team is onboarding new analysts who will be working with Vertex AI. The team lead wants everyone to understand the distinction between a foundation model and a large language model before they start building prompts.

Which statement BEST describes the relationship between these two concepts?

choices.text: A large language model is a type of foundation model trained on text data, whereas a foundation model is the broader category of large pretrained models that can span multiple modalities
choices.explanation: LLMs are a subset of foundation models focused on language.

choices.text: A foundation model is a model that has been fine-tuned on a specific task, while a large language model is always used in its original pretrained state
choices.explanation: This reverses the definitions — foundation models are pretrained base models, and fine-tuning is a separate step applied to them.

choices.text: A large language model and a foundation model are identical terms with no meaningful distinction between them
choices.explanation: LLMs are a specific subset of foundation models; the terms are not interchangeable.

choices.text: A foundation model can only process structured tabular data, while a large language model is restricted to generating code
choices.explanation: Foundation models span multiple modalities including text, image, and audio; neither definition is restricted this way.

questions.tip: Consider what the word 'foundation' implies about the scope of these models.
questions.explanation:
Foundation models are large pretrained models that serve as a base for many downstream tasks and can span modalities such as text, image, and audio. Large language models are a specific type of foundation model trained primarily on text.

**Why it works:** The relationship is one of subset and superset — every LLM is a foundation model, but not every foundation model is an LLM.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Reversing fine-tuning definitions: foundation models are the pretrained base, not the fine-tuned variant.
- Identical terms: LLMs are a specific subset.
- Restricted modalities: both descriptions are incorrect.

questions.question:
Following a board decision, a media company is adding an image-generation feature to its creative platform. The product team is evaluating which type of model to use and wants to understand the mechanism behind high-quality image synthesis from text prompts.

Which type of generative model progressively removes noise from a random signal to synthesise images?

choices.text: A diffusion model, which learns to reverse a noise-addition process to generate realistic images from a noisy starting point
choices.explanation: Diffusion models are defined by their iterative denoising process.

choices.text: A recurrent neural network, which generates images by predicting the next pixel in a sequence based on previous pixels
choices.explanation: RNNs process sequences but are not the basis for modern diffusion-based image synthesis.

choices.text: A multimodal foundation model, which stores a library of training images and retrieves the closest match to the text prompt
choices.explanation: Multimodal models generate new content; they do not perform retrieval from a stored library.

choices.text: A prompt-tuned language model, which converts the text prompt into an image by tokenising each word as a pixel coordinate
choices.explanation: Prompt tuning adjusts a model's soft prompts and does not produce images by mapping tokens to pixels.

questions.tip: The name of this model class describes what happens in the forward training pass.
questions.explanation:
Diffusion models are trained by gradually adding noise to data and then learning to reverse that process, allowing them to generate high-quality images from random noise guided by a text prompt.

**Why it works:** The denoising diffusion process is the mechanism behind models such as Imagen.

**Why the others don't work:**
- RNNs: not used for modern image diffusion.
- Multimodal model as retrieval system: incorrect; they generate, not retrieve.
- Prompt-tuned LLM mapping tokens to pixels: not how any model generates images.

questions.question:
The operations team is producing a glossary of gen AI terms for a company-wide training session. Two members of the team are drafting definitions for prompt engineering and prompt tuning and want to confirm they are distinct concepts.

Which TWO statements correctly distinguish prompt engineering from prompt tuning?

choices.text: Prompt engineering involves crafting or structuring the input text to guide a model's output without modifying any model weights
choices.explanation: Prompt engineering works at the input level and leaves the model unchanged.

choices.text: Prompt tuning involves adding trainable soft prompt tokens to the model's input and optimising them through gradient descent, while keeping the base model weights frozen
choices.explanation: Prompt tuning updates only the soft prompt parameters, not the full model.

choices.text: Prompt engineering requires retraining the full set of model weights on a labelled dataset before the new prompt can be used
choices.explanation: Prompt engineering requires no model training at all.

choices.text: Prompt tuning and prompt engineering are both zero-cost techniques that modify model architecture at inference time
choices.explanation: Prompt tuning involves a training step; neither technique modifies model architecture.

choices.text: Prompt engineering always produces better results than prompt tuning because it does not require any labelled data
choices.explanation: This is not a definition and the comparison is context-dependent.

questions.tip: Consider which technique touches model parameters and which touches only the input.
questions.explanation:
Prompt engineering and prompt tuning differ in whether model parameters are updated.

**Why it works:** Prompt engineering is purely about input design with no weight updates, while prompt tuning trains soft prompt vectors while keeping the foundation model frozen.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Prompt engineering requiring full retraining: incorrect, it needs no training.
- Both modifying architecture at inference: neither modifies architecture; prompt tuning trains soft tokens.
- Engineering always better: not a definitional distinction.

questions.question:
The engineering team is building a product recommendation engine on Vertex AI. The training dataset contains historical purchase records where each transaction is labelled with the customer's subsequent purchase. The team wants to train a model that maps each purchase history to the most likely next product.

Which machine learning approach BEST fits this requirement?

choices.text: Supervised learning, because the training data includes labelled examples that map inputs to known target outputs
choices.explanation: Labelled input-output pairs define supervised learning.

choices.text: Unsupervised learning, because the model must discover hidden purchase patterns without any labels in the dataset
choices.explanation: The dataset is explicitly labelled, ruling out unsupervised learning.

choices.text: Reinforcement learning, because the model receives a reward signal each time a customer clicks a recommended product in production
choices.explanation: The training described uses static labelled records, not a reward loop.

choices.text: Semi-supervised learning, because the labels are only partially complete and the model must infer the missing ones
choices.explanation: The scenario describes fully labelled data, not partial labels.

questions.tip: Focus on what the training data contains and how the model learns from it.
questions.explanation:
When every training example has a known target label, the approach is supervised learning.

**Why it works:** The labelled purchase histories provide direct input-output pairs the model learns to map, which is the definition of supervised learning.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Unsupervised: the data is already labelled.
- Reinforcement: requires a live reward signal, not static records.
- Semi-supervised: the scenario states fully labelled data.

questions.question:
The organization is looking to group its customer base into segments based on browsing behaviour, without defining the segments in advance. The data science team has unlabelled clickstream data and wants to find natural clusters to inform marketing strategy.

Which machine learning approach is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Unsupervised learning, which identifies patterns and structure in unlabelled data without predefined target categories
choices.explanation: Clustering unlabelled data to discover structure is the core use case for unsupervised learning.

choices.text: Supervised learning, which uses the clickstream data as input and the pre-defined customer segments as labels to train a classifier
choices.explanation: No predefined segments exist, so there are no labels to train against.

choices.text: Reinforcement learning, which assigns a reward when the clustering algorithm correctly identifies a customer segment
choices.explanation: Reinforcement learning requires an agent and a reward signal, not cluster discovery from static data.

choices.text: Transfer learning, which applies a model pretrained on labelled e-commerce data to generate segment labels for the unlabelled clickstream
choices.explanation: Transfer learning requires a compatible pretrained model and does not describe the unsupervised clustering task.

questions.tip: Consider which approach works without predefined categories or labels.
questions.explanation:
Discovering natural groupings in unlabelled data is the domain of unsupervised learning.

**Why it works:** Unsupervised methods such as clustering analyse data structure without needing target labels, which matches the unlabelled clickstream requirement.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Supervised: no segment labels exist.
- Reinforcement: no reward loop in this scenario.
- Transfer learning: requires a pretrained labelled model.

questions.question:
Management has decided to build an AI agent that learns to optimise data centre cooling settings by trying different configurations and observing the effect on energy consumption over time. The team is reviewing which machine learning concepts apply to this scenario before selecting a Vertex AI training strategy.

Which TWO statements correctly describe reinforcement learning as it applies to this scenario?

choices.text: The agent learns by taking actions in an environment and receiving a reward or penalty signal based on the outcome of each action
choices.explanation: Reward-based action-outcome feedback is the defining mechanism of reinforcement learning.

choices.text: The goal is to learn a policy that maximises cumulative reward over time, rather than to fit a static labelled dataset
choices.explanation: Maximising long-run reward through a learned policy is the objective of reinforcement learning.

choices.text: Reinforcement learning requires a fully labelled historical dataset of optimal cooling configurations before any training can begin
choices.explanation: Reinforcement learning does not require labelled data; it learns from environmental interaction.

choices.text: The model is trained by clustering similar cooling states together and assigning them the same configuration label
choices.explanation: Clustering is an unsupervised technique and does not describe reinforcement learning.

choices.text: Reinforcement learning converges instantly because the reward signal eliminates the need for iterative training
choices.explanation: Reinforcement learning is inherently iterative; convergence takes many episodes.

questions.tip: Focus on how the agent interacts with its environment and what it optimises.
questions.explanation:
Reinforcement learning is defined by an agent that learns through action-reward cycles to maximise cumulative reward.

**Why it works:** The cooling agent takes actions, observes energy outcomes as rewards, and updates its policy to maximise long-run efficiency.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Requires labelled dataset: reinforcement learning uses environmental feedback, not labels.
- Clustering with labels: describes unsupervised learning.
- Instant convergence: reinforcement learning requires many iterative episodes.

questions.question:
The operations team is designing an end-to-end ML pipeline on Google Cloud. Raw sensor readings arrive in a Cloud Storage bucket every hour, need to be cleaned and feature-engineered, and then fed into a training job. The team wants to identify which lifecycle stage each activity belongs to before choosing tools.

Which lifecycle stage does the cleaning and feature engineering work represent?

choices.text: Data preparation, which transforms raw ingested data into clean, structured features suitable for model training
choices.explanation: Cleaning and feature engineering are core data preparation activities.

choices.text: Data ingestion, which is the stage where raw data is moved from source systems into the ML platform
choices.explanation: Data ingestion covers moving data in; transformation happens in the next stage.

choices.text: Model training, which is the stage where the algorithm learns from the prepared features to produce model weights
choices.explanation: Model training consumes prepared features but does not include the preparation itself.

choices.text: Model management, which is the stage where trained models are versioned, monitored, and retired
choices.explanation: Model management occurs after deployment and covers governance of live models.

questions.tip: Consider which stage transforms raw data into the format a training job expects.
questions.explanation:
Data preparation sits between ingestion and training; it is where raw data is cleaned, normalised, and engineered into features.

**Why it works:** Cleaning and feature engineering convert raw sensor readings into the structured inputs a training algorithm can use, which is the definition of data preparation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Data ingestion: covers moving data, not transforming it.
- Model training: consumes prepared data but does not prepare it.
- Model management: post-deployment governance.

Management has decided to productionise a fraud detection model trained in Vertex AI. The model artefact has been validated and the team now needs to make it callable from the payment processing API. The team lead is mapping this work to the correct lifecycle stage.

Which lifecycle stage does exposing the model as a callable endpoint represent?

choices.text: Model deployment, where the trained model is made available as an endpoint that applications can call for predictions
choices.explanation: Serving the model via an endpoint is model deployment.

choices.text: Model training, where the validated artefact is retrained on production data before being served
choices.explanation: The model is already trained and validated; this step is about serving it.

choices.text: Data preparation, where the payment records are structured so the deployed model can accept them as inputs
choices.explanation: Data preparation precedes training and is not the same as deployment.

choices.text: Model management, where the endpoint is registered and versioned before any traffic is sent to it
choices.explanation: Registration and versioning are part of management, but making the model callable is deployment.

questions.tip: Consider which stage makes the model available for real-time inference.
questions.explanation:
Model deployment is the stage at which a trained model is hosted and made callable for inference.

**Why it works:** Exposing the model as an endpoint that the payment API can call is the purpose of model deployment.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Model training: the model is already trained.
- Data preparation: precedes training, not deployment.
- Model management: covers post-deployment governance such as versioning and monitoring.

questions.question:
The engineering team is building a legal document review assistant that must process entire contracts, some exceeding 300 pages, in a single prompt. The team is evaluating foundation models available in Vertex AI Model Garden and wants to choose the one MOST suited to this requirement.

Which selection factor is MOST critical for this use case?

choices.text: Context window size, because the model must fit the entire contract text into a single prompt without truncation
choices.explanation: A large context window is the primary requirement when processing long documents.

choices.text: Diffusion capability, because the model must generate images of each contract page for the review interface
choices.explanation: The task is text analysis, not image generation; diffusion models are irrelevant.

choices.text: Fine-tuning availability, because all foundation models must be fine-tuned on legal text before they can process any document
choices.explanation: Fine-tuning is not required for all use cases; context window is the critical factor here.

choices.text: Cost per token only, because long-context processing is equally well supported by all foundation models at any price point
choices.explanation: Not all models support long context; context window capability must be evaluated before cost.

questions.tip: Think about the technical constraint imposed by the document length.
questions.explanation:
When a task requires fitting very long input into a single prompt, context window size is the primary selection criterion.

**Why it works:** A model with an insufficient context window will truncate the contract, producing incomplete or inaccurate review results.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Diffusion capability: not relevant to text processing.
- Mandatory fine-tuning: not required for all tasks.
- Cost only: context window support varies and must be checked first.

questions.question:

The institution's compliance team requires that customer conversations cannot be used to train or improve any shared model, and that data residency must stay within a specific region.

Which model selection factor is MOST relevant to this requirement?

choices.text: Security and privacy controls, including data residency guarantees and isolation from shared model training pipelines
choices.explanation: Compliance constraints around data residency and training data isolation are security and privacy considerations.

choices.text: Modality support, because the chatbot must accept text and images simultaneously to serve the compliance requirement
choices.explanation: The compliance requirement is about data governance, not input modality.

choices.text: Context window size, because compliance conversations are typically longer than non-compliance conversations
choices.explanation: Context window is a performance factor, not a compliance or privacy factor.

choices.text: Fine-tuning availability, because the compliance team wants to retrain the model on anonymised conversations each quarter
choices.explanation: Quarterly fine-tuning is a separate consideration; the primary requirement is data isolation and residency.

questions.tip: Identify which selection factor maps to data governance and isolation requirements.
questions.explanation:
Regulatory requirements around where data is stored and how it is used map to the security and privacy factor in model selection.

**Why it works:** Choosing a model deployment that guarantees data residency and prevents conversation data from entering shared training pipelines directly addresses the compliance team's requirements.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Modality: the issue is data governance, not input types.
- Context window: a performance factor.
- Fine-tuning availability: a secondary consideration after privacy is satisfied.

Following a board decision, a retail company is selecting a foundation model in Vertex AI for a new product catalogue assistant. The assistant must accept both product images and descriptive text in the same prompt, and the business has a strict monthly AI budget cap.

Which TWO selection factors are MOST relevant to this scenario?

choices.text: Modality, because the assistant must accept both image and text inputs, requiring a multimodal model
choices.explanation: Combined image and text input requires a multimodal foundation model.

choices.text: Cost per token or per request, because the monthly budget cap constrains how much inference spend is acceptable
choices.explanation: A hard budget cap makes cost a primary selection factor.

choices.text: Diffusion architecture, because all models that accept image input are diffusion models
choices.explanation: Multimodal models are not necessarily diffusion models; diffusion is an image generation architecture.

choices.text: Reinforcement learning training history, because product catalogues require reward-based fine-tuning
choices.explanation: Training methodology is not a standard model selection factor for this use case.

choices.text: Context window size alone, because image inputs are always counted as zero tokens
choices.explanation: Image inputs do consume tokens in multimodal models; context window is relevant but not the primary factor here.

questions.tip: Match the two concrete requirements in the scenario to the selection factors that address them.
questions.explanation:
Modality and cost are the two factors directly driven by the scenario requirements.

**Why it works:** The multimodal input requirement demands a model that supports both image and text, and the budget cap makes cost-per-request a binding constraint.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Diffusion for image input: incorrect; multimodal and diffusion are different capabilities.
- Reinforcement learning history: not a standard selection factor.
- Context window alone: image tokens do count; context window is secondary here.

Which gen AI capability MOST directly enables this requirement?

choices.text: Personalised user experience, where gen AI generates individualised content and recommendations based on each user's history and preferences
choices.explanation: Dynamically tailoring content to an individual is the definition of personalised user experience.

choices.text: Text summarisation, where gen AI condenses each product description into a shorter version for faster page load

questions.tip: Look for the capability that adapts output to a specific individual rather than producing the same content for everyone.
questions.explanation:

questions.question:

Which data quality dimension is MOST directly affected by this finding?

choices.text: Completeness, because a significant portion of records lack values for a required feature column
choices.explanation: Missing values in required columns is the definition of a completeness issue.

choices.text: Consistency, because the missing values vary across different time periods within the dataset
choices.explanation: Consistency relates to whether values follow the same rules across records, not whether values are missing.

choices.text: Relevance, because contract length may not be relevant to predicting customer churn behaviour
choices.explanation: The scenario establishes that contract length is a key feature, so relevance is not the issue.

choices.text: Format, because the missing values are stored as empty strings instead of NULL markers
choices.explanation: The scenario describes missing values, not formatting differences in how missingness is represented.

questions.tip: Identify which dimension specifically measures whether all required data is present.
questions.explanation:
Completeness measures whether all required data is present in the dataset.

**Why it works:** Missing values in a key feature column directly indicate a completeness gap that must be addressed before training.

- Consistency: relates to value uniformity, not absence.
- Relevance: the column is established as relevant.

choices.text: Consistency, because the same value is represented in different formats across data sources
choices.explanation: Consistency captures whether equivalent values follow uniform representation rules.

choices.text: Completeness, because some records do not contain the customer's age at all
choices.explanation: All three sources contain the value; the issue is representation, not absence.

choices.text: Cost, because storing duplicate age values across three sources increases storage charges
choices.explanation: The issue is value representation, not storage cost.

choices.text: Availability, because the auditors had difficulty locating the age field across regions
choices.explanation: Availability addresses whether data can be accessed, not how values are formatted.

questions.tip: Look for the dimension that addresses whether values follow the same rules across the dataset.
questions.explanation:
Consistency measures whether the same logical values follow uniform representation across the dataset.

**Why it works:** Identical age values written in three different formats violate consistency, even if each individual record is technically present and accurate.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Completeness: the values are present.
- Cost: this is a quality issue, not a billing issue.
- Availability: the data is accessible; only the representation varies.

questions.question:

Which classification BEST describes this dataset?

choices.text: Structured data, because each record follows a predefined schema with fixed columns and data types
choices.explanation: Tabular data with a defined schema is structured data.

choices.text: Unstructured data, because the timestamps and customer IDs vary across rows
choices.explanation: Variation in row values does not make the data unstructured; the schema is consistent.

choices.text: Semi-structured data, because each row contains nested arrays of product categories
choices.explanation: The scenario describes flat columns, not nested structures.

choices.text: Binary data, because the transaction amounts are stored as numeric types
choices.explanation: Numeric storage does not classify data as binary; binary refers to formats like images or audio.

questions.tip: Focus on whether the data follows a predefined schema with consistent fields.
questions.explanation:
Structured data is organised in a fixed schema with predefined columns and types, typically stored in tables.

**Why it works:** A BigQuery table with consistent columns per row is the canonical example of structured data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Unstructured: the data has a clear schema.
- Semi-structured: no nested or variable structure is described.
- Binary: numeric columns are still structured, not binary blobs.

choices.explanation: Storage location does not determine data structure.

choices.text: Time-series data, because each file has a creation timestamp recorded in Cloud Storage
choices.explanation: Time-series describes ordered numeric measurements, not arbitrary timestamped files.

questions.tip: Identify the data type defined by the absence of a fixed schema in the content itself.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Structured: applies to schema'd content, not metadata around unstructured blobs.
- Tabular: the items are not rows in a table.
- Time-series: requires ordered numeric measurements over time.

questions.question:

choices.explanation: An associated category column is the definition of labelled data.

choices.text: Unlabeled data, because the photographs themselves are the input and contain no annotations within the image pixels
choices.explanation: Labels do not need to live within the image; an associated category column is sufficient.

choices.text: Synthetic data, because the categories were generated rather than naturally observed
choices.explanation: The scenario does not state the categories were synthetic; defective and non-defective are observed labels.

choices.text: Streaming data, because new photographs arrive continuously from the production line
choices.explanation: Streaming describes delivery method, not whether data has labels.

questions.tip: Look for whether each example carries a target value the model should learn to predict.
questions.explanation:
Labelled data has each example tagged with the target outcome the model should predict.

choices.explanation: Unsupervised methods are designed for unlabeled data exploration.

choices.text: Apply supervised classification, treating the email subject lines as automatic labels for the body text

choices.text: Apply reinforcement learning, treating each email as an environment state with a reward signal
choices.explanation: There is no reward signal in this scenario.

choices.text: Refuse to process the data because models cannot work without labels under any circumstances
choices.explanation: Many techniques work on unlabeled data, including clustering.

questions.tip: Consider which learning approach is designed for data without target labels.
questions.explanation:
Unlabeled data has no associated target categories, making it suitable for unsupervised methods such as clustering.

**Why it works:** Without labels, the model cannot learn input-to-target mappings, but it can discover structure or themes in the data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Subject lines as labels: subject lines are not consistent thematic categories.
- Reinforcement: no reward signal exists.
- Refusing entirely: unlabeled data has many valid use cases.

questions.question:
Following a board decision, an organisation is reducing privacy risk in a training dataset by replacing direct identifiers with non-reversible random tokens before the data is used to train a model.

Which privacy technique is being applied?

choices.text: Anonymisation, where identifiers are removed or transformed so that individuals cannot be identified from the data
choices.explanation: Replacing identifiers with non-reversible tokens to prevent re-identification is anonymisation.

choices.text: Pseudonymisation only, where identifiers are reversibly replaced with pseudonyms while a mapping is retained
choices.explanation: Pseudonymisation is reversible; the scenario describes non-reversible replacement, which is closer to anonymisation.

choices.text: Data duplication, where the dataset is copied multiple times for backup
choices.explanation: Duplication is not a privacy technique.

choices.text: Data labelling, where target categories are added to records
choices.explanation: Labelling is unrelated to privacy.

questions.tip: Identify the privacy technique that prevents re-identification.
questions.explanation:
Anonymisation removes or transforms identifiers so individuals cannot be re-identified.

**Why it works:** Replacing identifiers with non-reversible random tokens, with no mapping retained, is the canonical anonymisation pattern.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Pseudonymisation alone: reversible.
- Data duplication: not privacy.
- Data labelling: not privacy.

questions.question:
Management has decided to publish responsible AI guidance for the engineering organisation. The author wants two accurate principles to include.

Which TWO statements correctly describe responsible AI considerations?

choices.text: Accountability requires clear ownership and oversight of AI systems so that decisions can be reviewed and corrected when needed
choices.explanation: Accountability requires named owners and review mechanisms.

choices.text: Explainability helps users and stakeholders understand why an AI system produced a particular output
choices.explanation: Explainability addresses the why of model decisions.

choices.text: Bias in training data has no implications for model fairness as long as the model is large enough
choices.explanation: Bias in training data directly affects fairness, regardless of model size.

choices.text: Privacy is automatically guaranteed by AI models without any anonymisation or governance
choices.explanation: Privacy requires deliberate controls; it is not automatic.

choices.text: Transparency is unnecessary because AI systems are always trustworthy by default
choices.explanation: Transparency is necessary; trust is not automatic.

questions.tip: Look for the two accurate responsible AI principles.
questions.explanation:
Accountability and explainability are core responsible AI principles.

**Why it works:** Both directly support trustworthy and reviewable AI systems.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Bias has no implications: incorrect.
- Privacy automatic: incorrect.
- Transparency unnecessary: incorrect.
